Sharing results with a dashboard

Source: vignettes/articles/dashboards.Rmd
dashboards.Rmd

The workbench is for doing an analysis, and mv_report() writes a static record of it. mv_dashboard() fills the gap in between: a small, read-only app you can hand to people who do not use R, such as teachers, clients, committees or students, so they can explore the results themselves.

Build a dashboard

Fit a model as usual, then pass it to mv_dashboard():

library(mirtverse)

data <- key2binary(SAT12, key = c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,
                                  4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5))
mod <- mirt(data, 1, verbose = FALSE)

mv_dashboard(mod, title = "SAT12 results",
             subtitle = "Science test, 32 items, scored 0/1")

The dashboard opens in your browser. Assign it (app <- mv_dashboard(...)) if you want to keep it without opening it.

Choose the panels

Panel What it shows
"summary" Respondents, items, reliability and items to review, with the plain-language interpretation from interpret()
"items" The item table with a traffic-light status; select a row to see its item health card
"curves" Trace curves for chosen items and a slider that reads off the probabilities at any ability level
"information" Test information and standard error, and item information curves
"wright" The Wright map
"scores" The distribution of ability estimates and the sum-score conversion table
"persons" A searchable table of every person’s score, SE and percentile (off by default)
"dif" DIF results from dif()
"rt" Response-time results from fit_rt() 
res <- dif(data, group = gender)

mv_dashboard(mod, panels = c("summary", "items", "dif"), dif = res,
             title = "Fairness review", logo = "logo.png")

The curves, information, Wright map, scores and persons panels need a unidimensional model. For other models they are left out with a message.

Share it as one HTML file

The easiest way to share a dashboard is a single HTML file. It needs no server, no R and no internet connection, so you can email it, put it on a shared drive or a course page, and anyone can open it in a browser:

export_dashboard(mod, "sat12-dashboard.html", format = "html",
                 title = "SAT12 results")

It has the same panels as the app. The item table (sort, search, select an item to see its health card), the item curves with the ability slider, the item information curves and the person lookup all still work; the other plots are pictures. A file with item health cards for a long test can run to a few megabytes.

Share it as an app

A ‘shiny’ app needs a server to run on. export_dashboard() writes a folder that is ready to deploy:

export_dashboard(mod, "sat12-dashboard", title = "SAT12 results")

shiny::runApp("sat12-dashboard")          # try it locally
rsconnect::deployApp("sat12-dashboard")   # publish to shinyapps.io or Posit Connect

The folder holds app.R and dashboard.rds. The server installs mirtverse the same way you installed it, so install it from r-universe or GitHub, not from a local copy, before you deploy.

What the dashboard contains

Everything is computed once, when you build the dashboard; the app never refits or rescores anything, so it starts quickly. The saved dashboard holds only summaries: item statistics, parameters, curves, the binned score distribution and pictures of the item cards. It never holds the item responses.

Individual scores are included only when you add the "persons" panel, and export_dashboard() reminds you to check that you may share them. Use ids to show your own identifiers instead of row numbers:

mv_dashboard(mod, panels = c("summary", "persons"), ids = students$id)
